p1.title: Passage 1
paras: The slow dismantling of institutionalized stigmas surrounding mental health disorders is a significant cultural shift, yet clinical frameworks still struggle to address the deep structural root causes of psychological distress. For decades, public health messaging focused almost entirely on correcting chemical imbalances within individuals, promoting a pharmaceutical-first model of care. While biomedical interventions remain absolutely vital for millions, this narrow focus risks ignoring the socio-environmental factors—such as economic insecurity, chronic professional burnout, systemic marginalization, and the profound isolation of modern digital life—that drive psychological suffering. True mental healthcare requires moving past simple awareness campaigns toward dismantling the structural barriers that prevent access to care, specifically integrating psychiatric resources into primary public health networks. Furthermore, the growing commodification of "wellness" via digital platforms often reduces mental health care to a superficial aesthetic of self-care, masking the absence of systemic psychiatric support. The ultimate test of societal empathy lies in building accessible, communal, and non-punitive mental health infrastructure that values psychological well-being as a universal human right rather than an individual luxury.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: When self-help groups first spread through rural India, they were celebrated as a means of bringing credit to women whom banks had never considered worth the paperwork. A dozen women would meet weekly, pool small savings and lend to one another, and once the group had proven its discipline, a bank would extend a larger loan to it collectively. Repayment rates were remarkably high, for each member's reputation among her neighbours stood behind the debt. Many women used their first loans to buy a goat, a sewing machine or stock for a small shop, and some gained for the first time a measure of say in household decisions.

Success, however, attracted imitators less interested in empowerment than in profit. In several regions, commercial lenders competed to sign up borrowers, extending multiple loans to the same household at high rates of interest and enforcing repayment through public shaming. Debt that had once been a ladder became, for some, a trap. The lesson is not that small loans are harmful but that credit is a tool, not a cure. Without savings, training, access to markets and some protection against illness or crop failure, a loan merely transfers risk to those least able to bear it. The original groups worked because they were built on mutual trust; the mere imitation of their form could not reproduce it.

questions.q: The author criticizes a purely "pharmaceutical-first model of care" because it:
opts: Cannot treat chemical imbalances.
Risks overlooking the socio-environmental drivers of distress.
Relies too much on primary care.
Costs less than awareness campaigns.
questions.why: Detail: 'this narrow focus risks ignoring the socio-environmental factors'. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: Which is identified as a socio-environmental factor in mental health?
opts: Expansion of psychiatric infrastructure.
Genetic predisposition.
Economic insecurity and the isolation of digital life.
Wellness aesthetics in clinics.
questions.why: Detail: listed in the third sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: Digital "wellness" platforms can have a negative effect by:
opts: Reducing psychiatric care to a superficial, commercialised aesthetic of self-care.
Raising medicine prices.
Replacing primary health networks.
Making biomedicine obsolete.
questions.why: Detail: the fifth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: A critical step toward systemic mental healthcare, according to the text, is:
opts: Making individuals solely accountable.
Promoting wellness aesthetics.
Limiting messaging to biomedical explanations.
Integrating psychiatric resources into primary public health systems.
questions.why: Detail: the fourth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: The author's conclusion frames psychological well-being as:
opts: A universal human right needing accessible, communal infrastructure.
An individual responsibility managed through apps.
Secondary to physical health.
A luxury for rich societies.
questions.why: Main idea: the last sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
opts: Commercial lenders improved on the self-help group model.
Banks should stop lending to self-help groups.
Small loans are always harmful to poor households.
Group credit empowered rural women when built on trust and support, but profit-driven imitation made it harmful for some.
questions.why: Main idea: the original groups 'worked because they were built on mutual trust', while imitators 'less interested in empowerment than in profit' turned debt into 'a trap'.

questions.q: According to the passage, why were repayment rates in the early groups high?
opts: The government guaranteed every loan.
Banks charged very high rates of interest.
Lenders used public shaming to enforce repayment.
Each member's reputation among her neighbours stood behind the debt.
questions.why: Detail: 'for each member's reputation among her neighbours stood behind the debt'.

questions.q: The statement 'Debt that had once been a ladder became, for some, a trap' suggests that:
opts: credit that once helped women advance came to confine some borrowers in hardship.
borrowers used loans to buy ladders and tools.
all borrowers were eventually trapped by debt.
debt has never helped anyone improve their position.
questions.why: Inference: a ladder enables climbing; a trap holds one fast. The words 'for some' rule out 'all borrowers'.

questions.q: The author's stance on small loans is best described as:
opts: entirely hostile to all forms of small loans.
balanced, valuing the original model while criticising its profit-driven imitation.
indifferent to the outcome for borrowers.
uncritically supportive of commercial lenders.
questions.why: Tone: 'The lesson is not that small loans are harmful but that credit is a tool, not a cure.'

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'a measure of say' means:
opts: a legal right to vote
a precise quantity of speech
some degree of influence
an official position in the village
questions.why: Vocabulary: some women gained 'a measure of say in household decisions', i.e. a share of influence over them.
